title: Quantum gates with parametrically driven multi-qubit couplers
authors: Verena Feulner, Marjan Fani, Lukas Heunisch, Stephan Tasler, Michael J. Hartmann
abstract: Superconducting quantum processors could significantly profit from enhanced connectivity together with precise control of interactions and gates between qubits. Here we investigate plaquettes of four qubits that are coupled via a central tunable coupling circuit, so that not only gates between qubits connected by an edge of the plaquette can be executed but also between qubits across the diagonal. By numerically and analytically analyzing parametrically driven processes, we explore $\sqrt{\text{iSWAP}}$-gates between any pair of qubits, also across the diagonal, as well as three-qubit interactions and gates. For experimentally available circuit parameters, we for example find $\sqrt{\text{iSWAP}}$-gates with a gate time of 50 ns and 99.9\% fidelity, which is decreased to 99.4\% if two such gates are executed in parallel on disjoint qubit pairs in the plaquette. For three-qubit gates we find fidelities of 95\% fidelity at a gate time of 200 ns.
summary: The paper investigates using parametrically driven multi-qubit couplers (like SNAIL) to achieve high-connectivity gate operations on superconducting qubits. By analyzing the system Hamiltonian, the authors demonstrate methods to selectively activate two-qubit ($\sqrt{	ext{iSWAP}}$) and three-qubit gates across non-adjacent qubit pairs. This advances quantum computing hardware by providing pathways for complex interactions needed for quantum simulation.
main_problem: The primary challenge is enhancing connectivity and achieving high-fidelity quantum gates (two-qubit, three-qubit) in superconducting processors beyond nearest-neighbor interactions.
main_result: Multi-qubit couplers, such as the SNAIL circuit, enable all-to-all coupling within a plaquette, demonstrating $\sqrt{	ext{iSWAP}}$ and three-qubit gates with fidelities reaching 95% or higher.
method: The study employs numerical and analytical analysis of parametrically driven Hamiltonians, utilizing techniques like the Jacobi-Anger expansion to model time-dependent coupling strengths.
model_or_system: The system consists of superconducting transmon qubits coupled via tunable multi-qubit couplers (dc-SQUID or SNAIL). The Hamiltonian is controlled by external flux and AC driving fields to selectively activate desired interactions.
key_observables: Gate fidelity ($F$), gate time ($t_{	ext{gate}}$), resonance spread ($\Delta\omega$), and coupling strengths ($g_{12}, g_{123}$).
important_parameters: Asymmetry parameter ($\alpha$), external flux bias ($\phi_{	ext{dc}}$), drive amplitude ($\delta$), and qubit frequencies ($\omega_i$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often involves truncating the Hilbert space or using time-averaged approximations, which can lead to discrepancies when compared to full simulations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate circuit layouts (dc-SQUID, SNAIL), state population evolution during gate operations for various pairs/couplers, and plots showing coupling coefficients derived from Bessel functions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by introducing the physical platform and connectivity challenge, detailing the Hamiltonian modeling using both SQUID and SNAIL couplers, deriving the effective interaction strengths via normal mode analysis, and finally presenting fidelity benchmarks for two-qubit and three-qubit gates relevant to quantum simulation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations in superconducting quantum computing by engineering complex, tunable interactions necessary for advanced algorithms and simulations like Lattice Gauge Theories.
